newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian govt weakened but expected to win key vote.
newsitem.headline: Italian govt weakened but expected to win key vote.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi was expected to piece together his broken parliamentary majority on Thursday in a speech to the Senate, but commentators said deep problems would continue to hound his government.

Prodi has called confidence votes in both the upper and lower houses of parliament over the next three days after his hard left ally refused on Wednesday to back government plans to send a peacekeeping force to nearby Albania.

The security mission was salvaged when centre-right opposition parties grouped in the Freedom Alliance supported the government. In return for their help, they forced Prodi to hold a parliamentary vote to test his majority.
Prodi was due to address the upper house at around 12.30 p.m. (1030 GMT) and is expected to present the government's future policy plans on which the confidence votes will be based.

"Today in the Senate we will resolve everything," said Fausto Bertinotti, head of the hard-left Communist Refoundation party, which lies outside the coalition but secures its majority in the Chamber of Deputies (lower house).
Gianfranco Fini, head of the right-wing National Alliance, said he had no doubt Prodi would survive, adding that the opposition was in no hurry to tear down the coalition.

"Everyone knows the government will remain afloat for a few months with the help of Refoundation," Fini told a television chat show late on Wednesday. "We will let the majority cook in its own juices for a while."
Newspapers agreed that even if, as expected, Prodi pulls together his disparate majority, his government had been seriously wounded by the Albania stand-off.
"The political landscape for the majority born one year ago, is in pieces," left-leaning La Repubblica newspaper wrote in a front page editorial on Thursday.

Prodi's centre-left coalition came to power last May but has always struggled to come to terms with Refoundation, which rejected the Albania mission on ideological grounds and has similar strong views on important questions such as privatisations and reform of the state pensions system.
Refoundation chairman Armando Cossutta urged Prodi to keep his speech on Thursday as vague as possible, saying full policy plans on major issues facing Italy should be worked out later.
"If Prodi wants (to win) the confidence motion, then he should not enter into details," Cossutta told reporters.
But some of the coalition allies, fed up with Refoundation's unyielding stance, have called on Prodi to spell out clearly the government's programme.
"The government must go to parliament not with generic declarations, but precise, quantifiable plans," said Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini, head of the small centrist Italian Renewal Party.

Prodi himself was reported to be tired of dealing with the hard-left party. "I'm not prepared to muddle along. I want to find out if we can still govern with (Refoundation)," the prime minister was quoted as saying by La Stampa newspaper.
The confidence vote in the Senate was due to be held around 1930 GMT on Thursday while the vote in the lower house was scheduled for Saturday.
